items.title: MMX mission to reveal the origins of the Martian moons
items.summary: It was way back in the 1600s — immediately following the invention of the telescope — that moons around planets other than Earth were discovered. Jupiter’s four major moons were spotted by Galileo himself back in 1609 and 1610, leading his contemporary, Johannes Kepler, to hypothesize that the planet in between us and Jupiter — Mars — must have two moons of its own. Yet for centuries, no Martian moons were discovered. The first moons around Saturn were found later in the 17th century, and then Uranus and many of its moons were discovered in the 18th century. Even Neptune and its giant moon, Triton , were discovered back in 1846. Only in 1877 was Kepler’s hunch confirmed : when Asaph Hall spotted Mars’s two tiny satellites for the first time. The larger and innermore of Mars’s two moons, Phobos, is only 22.2 kilometers across, while smaller, more remote Deimos is just 12.6 kilometers wide. Both are very close to the red planet: Phobos completing an orbit every 7.66 hours at a mean distance of 9377 km from Mars’s center, and Deimos completing one every 30.35 hours at a distance of 23,460 km from the center of Mars. Although they’ve been observed remotely many times, these moons have never had an in situ mission dedicated to studying them before, and despite a plethora of indirect evidence, their origins remain uncertain. All of that is poised to change over the next few years, as JAXA’s MMX (Martian Moons eXplorer) mission now heads to Phobos and Deimos, where an orbiter, lander, rover, and sample return mission are all set to teach us more about these remote, tiny worlds than ever before. Here’s what lies in store. The relative sizes of the asteroid-like moons of Mars, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos is the innermost moon of Mars while the smaller Deimos is more than twice as far away. Despite their appearances as looking similar to asteroids, it’s thought that Phobos and Deimos were once joined by a larger, third, inner moon, which has since decayed and fallen back to Mars. All are thought to originate from a giant, ancient impact. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech It might sound like a bit of hyperbole, but when it comes to Mars, understanding its moons is the key to understanding the entire history of the red planet. There are two main scenarios for how these moons came to be, and they would both lead to entirely different planetary histories for the Mars, and determining as much as we can about which scenario occurred, and in as much detail as possible, is the whole goal of the MMX mission. The first major scenario for the Martian moons was the one that came along earlier in a chronological sense, and was focused on the size and shape of those moons: that they were captured asteroids. These small, irregular bodies have been discovered to have cratered surfaces, irregular shapes, and low densities: of around 1.8-1.9 g/cm³ for Phobos and around 1.5-1.7 g/cm³ for Deimos, which is comparable to rubble-pile asteroids. The second scenario is more recent, and instead suggests that, much like Earth’s moon, they were formed in the aftermath of a giant impact event. Even though the moons are small, they both orbit in the same plane as the Martian equator, have hints of the reddish color that’s the hallmark of Mars and orbit extremely close in to the red planet, whereas nearly all known captured bodies orbit considerably far out around the worlds that captured them. The possibility that these moons formed from a primordial circumplanetary disk around Mars has also been considered, but for such a small mass planet as Mars, isn’t a particularly viable scenario. Rather than only the two Martian moons we see today, Phobos and Deimos, a collision followed by a circumplanetary disk may have given rise to three moons of Mars, where only two survive today. The idea is that Mars’s once-innermost moon was destroyed and fell back onto Mars long ago. This hypothetical transient moon of Mars, proposed in a 2016 paper, is now the leading idea in the formation of Mars’s moons, and helps explain the enormous differences in topography between Mars’s northern and southern hemispheres. Credit : LabEx UnivEarthS | Université de Paris Diderot For a long time, there was a big problem with the second scenario: simulations of impacts would simply refuse to produce two small moons that were comparable to Phobos and Deimos. If you only produced small moons, they almost always wound up drifting farther away than even Deimos is located, while if you wanted to get multiple moons that were close in, they always wound up being larger. But then, in 2016, a remarkable new scenario was presented , which considered something novel: what if there was an ancient collision that created Phobos and Deimos, but also a third, much larger and more massive moon interior to them both, that has since been destroyed and fallen back onto Mars? All of a sudden, a bunch of puzzle pieces appeared to line up. Mars is one of the most unusual worlds in the Solar System in terms of its geography, with an enormous basin covering approximately half of the planet (the northern hemisphere) and elevated highlands covering the other half (the southern hemisphere), with an elevation difference of about 5 kilometers between the two. There’s one and only one very deep depression in the southern hemisphere, like a large chunk of material caused an ancient impact crater, but it’s the deepest point on the Martian surface by far. The Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) instrument, part of Mars Global Surveyor, collected over 200 million laser altimeter measurements in constructing this topographic map of Mars. The Tharsis region (center-left) is the highest elevation region on the planet, while the lowlands appear in blue. Note the much lower elevation of the northern hemisphere compared to the southern, with a mean difference in elevation of around ~5 km, thought to arise from the fallback of a third, large, former Martian moon. Credit : Mars Global Surveyor MOLA Team We have to keep in mind that the Solar System is old: between 4.5 and 4.6 billion years old, and that Mars has been this way for a very long time, for over 3 billion years at least. However, we are only seeing Mars as it is today; one of the difficulties we have with reconstructing the history of the Solar System is that we are only directly aware of the current survivors. We may have had more planets, moons, impacts, and rings around worlds in the distant past, but that evidence has largely been erased by the passage of time. Today, all that remains is the indirect evidence of their onetime presence, imprinted on whatever worlds, bodies, and features still persist. But there is a surefire way to tell whether the surviving moons of Mars are of asteroidal origin or whether they were formed by an impact that struck Mars: we can determine it the same way we determined that the Moon was formed by a giant ancient impact with Earth, by going there, landing on it, examining what we find, and bringing samples of it back home to analyze and compare it in a laboratory setting. If the material of Phobos and Deimos are different from the material found on Mars, they probably are captured bodies. But if the material is largely identical to the material we find on Mars itself, they’re almost certainly the result of an ancient impact. This close-up image of asteroid Itokawa was taken by the Hayabusa spacecraft in 2005 near its closest approach to the asteroid. Different parts of the asteroid have different densities, indicating that it formed as a contact binary from two predecessor “dirty snowball” asteroids, Itokawa likely has a history where several different smaller objects merged together to form what we see today: a common story among asteroid belt and Kuiper belt objects in our Solar System. items.title: How to experience more of reality
items.summary: What is reality? People have debated this for centuries. Is reality objective — something definite that exists independent of us? Or is it subjective, existing only in our individual heads? Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, argues it’s neither. Instead, she believes reality is relational. Relational reality explained So, what does relational reality mean? Barrett offers this example: Suppose you tell your therapist you’re mad, and they say you’re actually sad. An objective view might say there’s a correct answer — one of you is right, or perhaps both of you are wrong. Others would say the answer depends on each person’s individual experience. Barrett says it’s neither. “Reality may not be out there in the world, separate from you, and it’s definitely not only in your head,” she says. “It’s actually a combination of the two, which means that reality exists, but it exists in relation to you.” How the brain makes meaning Perception isn’t simply a faithful recording of the external world, Barrett explains. Rather, the brain draws on past experience to interpret incoming sensory signals, creating each individual’s very own Perception Box, the invisible mental frame through which we each experience the world. “Your box is the ingredients — the signals that you bring to creating the relational present,” Barrett says. To illustrate the idea, she turns to an old parable: If a tree falls in the forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? A relational realist would say a falling tree creates vibrations in the air, but those vibrations become sound only when an organism detects and interprets them, Barrett explains. Without an organism there to do so, the tree does not make a sound. Seeing beyond your own reality Different organisms have access to different signals. Animals have sensory surfaces that humans don’t, meaning aspects of reality available to them may be inaccessible to us. For example, in the ocean there are vibrations humans don’t detect that may be meaningful to whales. Their sensory systems allow them to experience signals that we don’t perceive, Barrett says. “We interfere with their ability to communicate with each other by our ignorance of their perspective,” Barrett says. That same idea can apply to interactions between humans. During an argument, people often appeal to the authority of objective reality to declare they’re right. But if reality is relational, you can’t do that. “In order to resolve the conflict, it means you have to admit the idea that somebody else’s experience has equivalent authority to your own,” Barrett says. “The idea that somebody else’s experience is part of reality as much as yours doesn’t invalidate your experience. It means that your experience is a part of reality, but it’s not the only part.” How to expand your Perception Box According to Barrett, some aspects of reality are shared, while others are accessible to one person but not another. Exposure to different people and experiences can give us access to new signals and meanings, expanding the aspects of reality available to us. Spend most of your time around people who are just like you — who have similar reactions and experiences — and you’ll likely reinforce the remembered past that’s easy for you to conjure. But if you’re curious and foraging for new sets of signals and new meanings, you’re likely to expand the aspects of reality that you have access to. “The goal there is to be curious and be humble,” Barrett says. “As a person, I think it’s incumbent upon us. We really ought to experience as many aspects of reality as we can. Otherwise, we’re ignorant, and ignorance is not helpful.” We interviewed Lisa Feldman Barrett for Relational Realism , a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators . As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch the first episode above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series. This video How to experience more of reality is featured on Big Think .

items.title: I Cannot Make My Son Purer Than This Sickening World
items.summary: “Everything” by Ingeborg Bachmann, translated by Philip Boehm and Tess Lewis When we sit down to eat like two people turned to stone or when we meet at the door to the apartment in the evening because we both thought to lock it at the same time, I feel our grief stretching like a bow from one end of the world to the other—in other words, from Hanna to myself—a bow that is drawn and fitted with an arrow that must fly straight to the heart of the unmoved heavens. When we walk back through the front hall she’s two steps ahead of me, she goes into the bedroom without saying “Good night” and I flee to my room, to my desk, where I stare into space, her lowered head before my eyes and her silence in my ears. Is she lying down and trying to sleep or is she awake and waiting? What for?—since she isn’t waiting for me! When I married Hanna it was less about her than because she was pregnant. I didn’t have a choice, I didn’t have to make a decision. I was moved because something new was coming into being, something that came from us, and because I felt the world was waxing. Like the moon, when it appears new and tender with a wisp of color at the start of its course and it is customary to bow three times. I experienced moments of absentmindedness I hadn’t known before. Even in the office—although I had more than enough to do—or during a conference I was suddenly transported into a state where I was focused solely on the child, this unknown, unreal being, heading toward him with all my thoughts, all the way to the warm, lightless womb where he lay confined. The child we were expecting changed us. We hardly went out anymore, and neglected our friends; we found a bigger apartment, furnished it better, and ensconced ourselves more permanently. But everything began to change on account of the child I was waiting for: I stumbled on thoughts the way you stumble onto a mine, unexpectedly—thoughts of such explosive power that they should have made me recoil, but I went on, with no sense of the danger. Hanna misunderstood me. Because I couldn’t decide whether the stroller should have big or small wheels, I appeared to be indifferent. (I really don’t know. Whatever you think. Yes, I’m listening.) When I stood there idly in the stores where she was picking out bonnets, jackets, and diapers, hesitating between pink and blue, synthetic wool and real wool, she accused me of being distracted, of not being engaged. But I was engaged, and far too much. How can I possibly express what was going on inside me? I felt like a wild man who suddenly discovers that the world in which he moves—between firepit and campsite, between sunrise and sunset, between hunting and eating—is also the world that is millions of years old and that will disappear, that its place is insignificant among many solar systems, that it is spinning around itself and orbiting the sun at great speed. All of a sudden I saw myself in other contexts, myself and the child, who at a particular time in early or mid-November was supposed to begin his turn at life, exactly as I once had, as had everyone before me. It just has to be properly visualized. This whole lineage! Like picturing black and white sheep before you fall asleep (a black one, a white one, a black one, a white one, and so on)—sometimes this can make you dull and drowsy but at other times it can keep you desperately awake. This formula for falling asleep has never worked for me, although Hanna, who learned it from her mother, swears that it’s more relaxing than a sleeping pill. Perhaps many find it relaxing to think about this series: And Shem begat Arphaxad. And Arphaxad lived five-and-thirty years, and begat Salah. And Salah begat Eber. And Eber begat Peleg. And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu, and Reu begat Serug, and Serug begat Nahor, and later each begat many additional sons and daughters, and the sons kept begetting sons, namely Nahor begat Terah and Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran. I tried a few times to think through the entire lineage, not only forward but also backward, all the way to Adam and Eve, from whom we are unlikely descended, or to the hominids, who may be our forebears, but in each case the chain gets lost in obscurity, and so it doesn’t matter whether you cling to Adam and Eve or to some other pair. However, if you prefer not to cling at all and instead ask to what end each of them was given their turn, then this whole chain doesn’t make any sense and you have no idea what to make of all the begettings or the first and last lives. Because each person gets only one turn for the game that he stumbles upon and is called on to understand: procreation and upbringing, economics and politics, and he is allowed to busy himself with money and feelings, with work and invention and the justification of the rules of the game called thinking. But we probably just have to come to terms with the fact that we keep multiplying with such confidence. The game needs players. (Or do the players need the game?) I, too, had been placed in the world with such confidence, and now I had placed a child in the world. And now the thought was making me shiver. I started seeing everything in relation to the child. My hands, for example, that were destined to touch and hold it, our fourth-floor apartment on Kandlgasse, the Seventh District, the streets that crisscrossed the city down to the Prater meadows, and finally the entire overcrowded world that I would teach him about. The child should hear the names from me: table and bed , nose and foot . Also words such as: spirit and God and soul , useless words in my opinion, but you can’t exactly hide them, and later on, words as complicated as: resonance , diapositive , chiliasm , and astronautics . I would need to make sure my child finds out what everything means and what everything is used for, a door handle and a motorcycle, a mouthwash and a questionnaire. My head was spinning. Of course, when the child came I had no use for big lessons. There he was, wrinkled, jaundiced, pitiful, and there was one thing I wasn’t prepared for—that I had to give him a name. Hanna and I hastily came to an agreement, and we had three names entered in the register: my father’s, her father’s, and my grandfather’s. But we didn’t end up using any of these names. By the end of the first week his name was Fipps. I don’t know how that was decided. It might have been partly my fault, because, along with Hanna, who was inexhaustible when it came to inventing and mixing nonsensical syllables, I tried calling him nicknames—his actual names were clearly not suitable for this tiny naked creature. After all our fawning, Fipps was the name that emerged, which has irritated me more and more with every passing year. At times I even blamed the child, as if he could have defended himself, as if it hadn’t all happened by chance. Fipps! I’ll have to keep calling him that, and so make him seem ridiculous even beyond the grave, and us as well. When Fipps lay awake or asleep in his blue-and-white crib, when I was only good for wiping some spittle or sourish milk from his mouth or for picking him up when he started crying, hoping to provide some relief, it first occurred to me that he, too, had plans for me, but that he was giving me time to figure it out, that he absolutely wanted to give me time, like a specter that appears to someone before withdrawing into the darkness, then reappears with the same indecipherable expression. I often sat next to his bed, looking down on that face that seemed so impassive and into those eyes that gazed in no direction, studying his features like a script that had been handed down with no key to decipher its meaning. I was happy to see how steadfastly Hanna tended to the obvious matters, nursing him, putting him to sleep, waking him up, transferring him, and changing his diaper as prescribed. She cleaned his nose with little cotton swabs and dusted between his chubby thighs with a cloud of powder,

items.title: Like Yesteryear, but Better
items.summary: How’s this for a job offer? In the span of no more than 10 years, you’re to have seven babies for C-suite women at a major tech firm. You’ll be on a strict diet and exercise regime, your vitals constantly monitored. You can’t have sex. Or a C-section (lest you forgo the “natural birth bonus”). Nor can you tell your loved ones what your actual job is (as far as they’re concerned, you’re in “consulting”). You’ll get just six months of downtime between pregnancies. And, as the test case for this “groundbreaking pilot program” to make The Company “the world’s most equitable workplace,” you’ll earn more than a million dollars. In Natalie, the narrator of Sarah Anderson’s very funny debut novel, Fallow , The Company finds a taker—one who isn’t, readers soon discover, quite the sucker she may seem to be. She’s a recent college graduate, wryly aware that she is not the typical striver. Motherhood versus career is not a dilemma that haunts her, which gives her an unusually deadpan perspective on angst about work-life balance. Anderson does more than skewer corporate posturing; she shows Natalie stumbling into unexpected insights about freedom and entrapment. At 23, Natalie is employed in a soulless call center, fielding complaints on a hotline for disgruntled employees in many spheres, but when her family expresses concern about her future, she says, “I don’t need a path. I have a path. I just need money.” Her job has enough upsides—flexible hours, livable pay, and her friend Libby, who “regularly dosed the communal break-room coffee with CBD oil”—that she might have languished in it forever. But then her wisdom teeth start wreaking havoc and she’s forced to find work that comes with dental insurance. That’s when she happens on the position at The Company. Natalie, of all people, should be wary of the offer, with its unorthodox contract and its demand for real body-morphing labor . After all, at the call center she’s had to listen to endless complaints about work life (from “disputes between coworkers over fridge real-estate” to “accidents caused by coked-out managers operating heavy machinery”). And, as one of 11 sisters, she’s seen firsthand what multiple pregnancies can do to a woman. Throughout Natalie’s childhood, her mother was “tired and round and looking for a bathroom, body waxing and waning like the moon.” But she is broke and her jaw is aching, so Natalie convinces herself that a job at The Company isn’t so bad. Seven is four fewer kids than her mom carried for free, plus, she thinks, “I didn’t even have to do the hardest part; I didn’t have to keep the babies.” Staring at the contract’s $700,000 completion bonus, she begins to see the role as a way to earn enough money to opt out for good: “a basic Would You Rather—­one decade of my body to win back the rest of my life.” (This being the 2020s, she’s also swayed by the $60,000 cosmetic-surgery bonus. She pictures herself, postpartum, a decade hence: “Thighs slender and firm, colt-like, a gap between them through which light could shine upon every person who stood before me.”) In prose that is sharp and entertaining, Anderson refreshingly takes on several familiar themes at once: the hidden tolls that working women still face, the stranglehold of Big Tech, the Orwellian nature of corporate-speak , the relentless self-monitoring of wellness culture . Her unifying conceit is that the ideal of “having it all” is not just impossible to neatly pull off, but impossible to simply escape. If you’re thinking, Wait, we’ve been here recently , perhaps you’ve read Caro Claire Burke’s Yesteryear , a debut that sold more than 1 million copies within a few months of its release last spring. Burke’s narrator, also named Natalie, is a young Christian tradwife influencer whose lifestyle, as shown on Instagram, is a carefully curated middle finger to the having-it-all quest. Yet as both her influencer business and her family boom, she finds herself caught in a twisted version of just that ideal: the resentful mother of many kids and the secret, stressed-out breadwinner. [ Read: What happens when the tradwife dream goes wrong? ] From the start, Yesteryear ’s narrator seems like little more than her author’s puppet, a caricature devised to puncture the tradwife fervor of the past few years. This kind of formulaic flatness could easily have befallen the people employed by The Company—an Amazon-esque behemoth that “did everything, everywhere, their logo as familiar as your own name.” Instead, Anderson gives revealing cameos to quirky figures, including Shane, the conniving but guileless SVP of People Experience who toggles between HR euphemisms and saying the quiet part out loud. In a presentation about the company’s mission to enhance gender equity through surrogacy, he itemizes how taxing pregnancy can be for a woman and her colleagues alike. “Nausea, exhaustion, bathroom breaks, brain fog—it’s hard on everyone,” he laments. The long-term goal (drastically cutting parental leave) goes unstated at first, but he lets slip that the short-term aim isn’t exactly altruistic, either: An executive named Valerie is “the perfect candidate for the launch,” he tells Natalie, because she was “frankly a nightmare to be around” during her first pregnancy. Then there’s Astrid, Natalie’s “minder,” a 20-something Scandinavian woman who adds a passive-aggressive energy to Natalie’s mandated workouts, “slowly edging her treadmill speed and incline just past mine, always doing an extra crunch.” Meanwhile, Astrid’s massages feel “80 percent vindictive, 20 percent transformative”—the corporate lean-in ethos (quite literally) operating even among the lowly ranked. Anderson’s greatest feat of character construction is Natalie herself, particularly her voice. She tosses off clever metaphors for her situation. Pregnancy, for example, becomes a housing issue. Weeks after her first delivery, her body is a “slightly looser, wetter version of itself, a room with non-catastrophic water damage.” Summing up the deal she’s struck—constant surveillance and social isolation in exchange for money and a luxury condo with minimalist decor—she remarks, “I myself was a fetus, in a particularly tasteful womb.” When Shane suddenly announces that she’s required to be in the office three days a week, Natalie reports to work to pursue her pregnancy regimens in view of her “colleagues,” becoming a working mother in an unfamiliar sense: maternity operating according to a calibrated plan. Natalie’s office door is marked Development Manager , and the children she bears fall under “Deliverables” in her performance reviews—biology blurring into corporate strategy, life reduced to a measurable output from the very beginning. (Anderson’s vision is at once outlandish and recognizable: More than a few companies have been known to offer parents perks, including breast-milk delivery for moms on business trips, with the ulterior motive of maximizing productivity.) Fascinated and repelled by the way the spheres of work and life converge, Anderson gives Natalie a chance to push back—and to discover the difficulty of doing so. Natalie lives for the “fallow periods” between pregnancies, when she’s left to her own devices and structure falls away. Astrid is gone, and so are the Pyrex dishes of healthy food in her company-provided fridge. She gets drunk and high, has sex, and eats mountains of junk. Each time, she’s surprised by the darker feelings that bubble up: “the sadness of excess, a feeling in my brain of bottoming out.” The realization slowly dawns on her that she’s losing touch with her sole friend, Libby, and the one sister she’s close to (the rest are a blur). Still, Natalie considers these rebellious bursts “sacred,” exhilarated by the sensation that she’s “moving the plot”—even as we watch her cyclical existence get subsumed into the company agenda, which calls for her to be the “best possible vessel.” After her benders, she “atone[s]” with yoga, acupuncture, and spa tr

items.title: Computer Chips Are the Most Magnificent Things Humanity Has Ever Made
items.summary: They power our phones, cars, dishwashers—and the A.I. systems that prop up the economy. They’re also at the heart of fierce geopolitical rivalry.
items.title_original: Computer Chips Are the Most Magnificent Things Humanity Has Ever Made
items.title_en: Computer Chips Are the Most Magnificent Things Humanity Has Ever Made
items.title_zh: 计算机芯片是人类有史以来创造的最伟大的发明——它们驱动着我们的手机、汽车、洗碗机，以及支撑经济运行的人工智能系统。它们也是激烈地缘政治竞争的核心。

items.title: Everyone Can Be Migos Now
items.summary: The viral “Hotel Lobby” meme, which lets users inhabit the bodies of Quavo and Takeoff using A.I., resembles a kind of digital blackface, but also speaks to a technology that makes appropriation the default.
items.title_original: Everyone Can Be Migos Now
items.title_en: Everyone Can Be Migos Now
items.title_zh: 现在谁都能成为Migos了——那款风靡网络的“酒店大堂”梗图，让用户能通过人工智能化身为Quavo和Takeoff，这既类似于一种数字版的“黑脸”行为，同时也反映出一种将文化挪用视为常态的技术。

items.title: When God Is Another Addiction
items.summary: A remarkable memoir recounts a writer’s struggles with alcoholism and religious faith—and the unsettling ways in which each has fed her longing for the other.
items.title_original: When God Is Another Addiction
items.title_en: When God Is Another Addiction
items.title_zh: 《当上帝成为另一种瘾》——这部非凡的回忆录讲述了一位作家在酗酒与宗教信仰之间的挣扎，以及二者如何以令人不安的方式相互助长，加剧了她对另一方的渴求。
